clue.text: Top courier lost somewhere in the Antilles

indicators.note: something lost has gone astray, so these letters have wandered out of their proper order

parts.note: the ten letters of both words, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A senior delivery driver has gone astray somewhere in the Caribbean islands.
explanation.definitionFit: The Caribbean island territory belongs to the Greater Antilles chain, so it is one place within that group.

clue.text: Bolts, being cut up

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means the word is written from the bottom, so its letters run backwards

parts.note: to snip is to cut with scissors

explanation.surface: Bolts are being sawn through or chopped into pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut up' looks like one phrase meaning chopped, but 'up' is separate and turns SNIP into PINS.
explanation.definitionFit: Pins and bolts are both metal rods used to fasten things together, so the plural nouns are close synonyms.

clue.text: Neurotic hides cash

indicators.note: the word that hides something keeps it tucked away inside its own letters

parts.note: the four letters after the opening N

explanation.surface: An anxious person keeps money stashed away out of sight.
explanation.definitionFit: The single European currency is money, so a quantity of it counts as cash.

clue.text: One of a crew to cause online offence on empty vacuous platform

parts.note: to troll is to post deliberately provocative messages on the internet

indicators.note: vacuous means emptied of its contents, so only the outside letters of the word before it survive

parts.note: the first and last letters of this word
a dolly is a wheeled platform, such as the one a film camera rides on

explanation.surface: Some crew member stirs up trouble on the internet from an empty and pointless stage.
explanation.walkthrough: TROLLEY DOLLY is British slang, a little mocking, for a flight attendant, who pushes the drinks trolley down the aisle.
explanation.definitionFit: A flight attendant belongs to an aircraft's cabin staff, so is one member of that airline team.

clue.text: Touch up a painting of deranged headless forester

indicators.note: deranged means disordered, so the remaining letters are put into a fresh order
a headless word has lost its first letter

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A mad woodsman sets about retouching a canvas.
explanation.definitionFit: Conservators bring a damaged artwork back to its original condition, which is what retouching a canvas means.

clue.text: Eastwood close to becoming president

parts.note: Clint Eastwood, the film actor and director
on can mean beside or next to, as in a town on the coast

explanation.surface: The film star Eastwood is on the verge of being elected head of state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close to' looks like an instruction to take a last letter, but here it simply means ON.
explanation.definitionFit: Bill Clinton served as the forty-second head of state of the United States.

clue.text: Tom Baker, to start with, is grave

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: what comes to start with is the opening letter only

parts.note: the opening letter of this surname

explanation.surface: The actor Tom Baker, known for Doctor Who, starts off looking serious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grave' poses as the adjective solemn, but it is the noun, a burial place.
explanation.definitionFit: A tomb is a burial chamber or vault, so it is a place where someone is interred like a grave.

clue.text: Tax excessively deliveries by coach

parts.note: in cricket an over is a set of six balls bowled, so overs are groups of deliveries
to coach someone is to train them

explanation.surface: Couriers are being charged too much tax on parcels sent by bus.
explanation.definitionFit: To tax here is to strain or burden, so pushing something beyond its limits is to strain it too far.

clue.text: Make call to your lady, answering initially with expression of disgust and roar

parts.note: to bell someone is British slang for phoning them

indicators.note: initially points to the first letter of each of the words before it

parts.note: the opening letters of these three words
ugh is what you say when revolted

explanation.surface: Someone phones a woman, who answers with a disgusted noise and a shout.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'give someone a bell' is everyday British for phoning them.
explanation.definitionFit: A loud hearty laugh is a roar of laughter, so roar can stand for this deep laugh.

clue.text: It uncovers having the heebie-jeebies!

indicators.note: someone with the heebie-jeebies is jittery and jumpy, so the letters jump about out of order

parts.note: the ten letters of both words, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A twitchy habit gives away that someone is scared stiff.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and the definition: a nervous twitch reveals that its owner is anxious.
explanation.definitionFit: An involuntary twitch betrays anxiety, so it is the thing that exposes someone suffering from the jitters.

clue.text: Duck spotted regularly in The Mall

indicators.note: seen at regular intervals means taking every other letter of the words that follow

parts.note: the first, third, fifth and seventh letters; The Mall is the grand avenue leading to Buckingham Palace in London

explanation.surface: A duck has been seen now and again along The Mall in London.
explanation.definitionFit: The teal is a small freshwater dabbling bird of the duck family.

clue.text: Catcall girl at first; that is, make a play for girl at first, skipping (oddly) wine and music

parts.note: a jeer from a crowd

indicators.note: at first keeps just the opening letter of the word before it

parts.note: the first letter of this word
i.e., the abbreviation of Latin id est
to woo is to court someone

indicators.note: skipping the odd-numbered positions leaves only the even-placed letters

parts.note: the first letter again
the second and fourth letters

explanation.surface: A man whistles at a girl, chats her up, and offers her wine and music.
explanation.definitionFit: Boogie-woogie is a fast blues piano style, a kind of music popular in the 1930s and 40s.

clue.text: Composition of Kern: 'Tolstoy, Russian Icon'

indicators.note: a composition is something put together, so these letters are assembled into something new

parts.note: the eleven letters of the two names, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A piece by the composer Jerome Kern titled after the great Russian novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Composition' suggests a song by Kern, but it is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bolshevik revolutionary leader is an iconic figure of twentieth-century Russian history.

clue.text: Fats Waller treated for cataracts

indicators.note: something treated has been worked on and processed, so these letters are reworked

parts.note: the jazz pianist's ten letters, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: The jazz pianist Fats Waller undergoes surgery for an eye condition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cataracts' wants to be the eye disorder, following 'treated for', but it means great cascades of water.
explanation.definitionFit: A cataract is also a large steep cascade of a river, so the plurals are synonyms.

clue.text: Novel describing Cameron becoming Tory leader?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an E. M. Forster novel of 1910
second meaning: Michael Howard led the Conservative (Tory) party until David Cameron replaced him in 2005, ending his leadership

explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as possessive: Cameron's election finished the leadership of his predecessor.
explanation.definitionFit: Forster's story of the Schlegel sisters and a country house is a classic English book, and the phrase also names the finish of a politician's tenure.

clue.text: One of the faithful seen back in rickety local

indicators.note: back means the letters are read from right to left
the answer can be seen within the run of words that follows
in tells you the letters sit inside the following words

parts.note: letters straddling the two words

explanation.surface: A regular drinker is spotted back in the run-down pub.
explanation.walkthrough: A local is a British pub near home. Reading backwards through the phrase finds the word.
explanation.definitionFit: An acolyte is a devoted follower or an assistant in church services, so one of a body of believers.

clue.text: Farage cut off before broadcast about African country

indicators.note: cut off means the final letter is lopped from the name

parts.note: Nigel Farage is a British politician, a leading campaigner for Brexit

indicators.note: about means turned round, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: to air a programme is to broadcast it

explanation.surface: Farage is taken off air ahead of a programme about an African nation.
explanation.definitionFit: Nigeria is the most populous nation in West Africa.

clue.text: Cockney's a tool, they say, with charm

indicators.note: a Cockney Londoner drops the h from words, so we hear his pronunciation
they say points to how the words sound when spoken

parts.note: a hammer, with the h dropped in Cockney style

explanation.surface: A Londoner is called an idiot but has plenty of charisma.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A tool' looks like an insult, a fool, but it is a hammer. Cockney is the working-class East London accent, famous for dropping h.
explanation.definitionFit: To enamour is to captivate someone and make them fond, so it is a verb close to charm.

clue.text: Having drunk a litre — about a litre — finally appreciate beer

indicators.note: something that has drunk a thing holds it inside itself

parts.note: re means concerning
A plus L, the symbol for litre

indicators.note: finally keeps only the very last letter of the next word

parts.note: the last letter of this word
A plus L again, swallowed by the rest

explanation.surface: After downing about a litre each, someone finally appreciates a good beer.
explanation.walkthrough: There are two 'a litre's: the second joins the charade, and the first is the one swallowed, sitting just inside the final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Real ale is traditional cask-conditioned British beer, promoted by the Campaign for Real Ale.

clue.text: Rendezvous with Everyman after work — get in!

parts.note: the setter, Everyman, refers to himself as me

indicators.note: work here is an instruction to work on the following letters, reshaping them

parts.note: these five letters, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A date with the setter after office hours – and it is a success!
explanation.walkthrough: The setter's pen name stands for ME, a common crossword convention. 'Get in!' is a British cheer of triumph.
explanation.definitionFit: A rendezvous is an arranged encounter at a set time and place, the same as an appointment to see someone.

clue.text: Samiest, re-hashed figure in collage

indicators.note: rehashed material is reworked into a new form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: The most repetitive material, recycled, forms a figure in a collage.
explanation.definitionFit: Henri Matisse, the French painter, made famous late works from cut-out paper, making him a leading figure of the form.

clue.text: Revolutionary for citadels to be overthrown

indicators.note: something overthrown is toppled and thrown into disarray, so the letters lose their order

parts.note: the eleven letters of both words, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A rebel leader calls for the fortresses to be toppled.
explanation.definitionFit: Fidel Castro led the Cuban uprising of 1959 and then governed Cuba for decades.

clue.text: Clue: sidearm's concealed

indicators.note: concealed means kept inside out of sight, so the letters lie within the word

parts.note: the letters between S and RM

explanation.surface: A tip-off: the pistol is hidden on someone's person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clue' looks like crossword self-reference, but it means a notion, as in 'I haven't a clue'.
explanation.definitionFit: Having no clue means having no notion, so the two nouns are synonyms for a thought or inkling.

clue.text: Fairy-tale figure masticating gore

indicators.note: masticating means chewing, and chewed-up letters come out mangled into a different order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A storybook monster munches on bloody flesh.
explanation.definitionFit: Ogres are man-eating giants that appear in folk stories such as Jack and the Beanstalk.

clue.text: Stagger backwards giving lecherous gaze

indicators.note: backwards means the letters are written from right to left

parts.note: to reel is to stagger

explanation.surface: A drunk lurches back while ogling someone.
explanation.definitionFit: A leer is a sly suggestive look, the kind of lustful stare the clue describes.

clue.text: Troubled? Assuage trouble with a pet

indicators.note: troubled means disturbed, so the following word's letters are stirred up

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
to dog someone is to plague or trouble them

explanation.surface: Feeling anxious? Soothe your worries with an animal companion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Troubled?' and 'trouble' look like a matched pair, but the first rearranges and the second is DOG. A sausage dog is a dachshund.
explanation.definitionFit: The dachshund, nicknamed for its long body, is a common household companion animal.

clue.text: Audibly expressed frustration with BBC4, perhaps

indicators.note: audibly means as heard, so we want a word that is pronounced like the next phrase

parts.note: breathed out in exasperation

explanation.surface: Someone groans aloud at what is showing on BBC Four.
explanation.walkthrough: BBC Four is a British television channel; in dated British slang a channel is a side, as in 'switch to the other side'.
explanation.definitionFit: Older British speakers call a TV channel a side, so one particular station is an example.

clue.text: Ant's friend, celeb: 'Unlimited speed? Slow down!'

parts.note: Ant and Dec are a British TV presenting duo

indicators.note: without limits means losing both outer edges, keeping only the middle letters

parts.note: the inner letters with the first and last removed
rate means pace or speed

explanation.surface: A TV star's sidekick is told to ease off after racing at full pelt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unlimited speed' reads as one phrase, but 'Unlimited' trims celeb, and speed stands alone.
explanation.definitionFit: To decelerate is to reduce velocity, which is exactly what slowing down means.
